content: Surfactant replacement therapy has been shown to be effective in preventing and treating neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). A deficiency or dysfunction of surfactant can also contribute to respiratory failure in other conditions, such as meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS). This study aimed to assess the impact of surfactant administration in the treatment of late preterm and term infants diagnosed with MAS. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies from 1985 to December 2006. Additional sources such as previous reviews, conference proceedings, expert informants, and journal handsearching were also utilized. An updated search was performed in November 2014, including clinical trial registries like ClinicalTrials.gov, Controlled-Trials.com, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. The analysis included only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the effects of surfactant therapy in late preterm and term infants with MAS. The data collected focused on clinical outcomes such as mortality, the need for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), pneumothorax, duration of assisted ventilation, duration of supplemental oxygen, intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) of any grade or severe IVH, and chronic lung disease. The analysis adhered to the standards set by the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. Four randomized controlled trials, involving a total of 326 infants, met the inclusion criteria. The meta-analysis of these trials revealed no statistically significant effect of surfactant therapy on mortality (risk ratio [RR] 0.98, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.41 to 2.39; risk difference [RD] 0.00, 95% CI -0.05 to 0.05). There was no heterogeneity observed for this outcome (I² = 0%). However, the meta-analysis of two trials (208 infants) demonstrated a significant reduction in the risk of requiring ECMO with surfactant therapy (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.91; RD -0.17, 95% CI -0.30 to -0.04). The number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) was 6 (95% CI 3 to 25). There was no heterogeneity for the RR (I² = 0%), but moderate heterogeneity was noted for the RD (I² = 50%). One trial involving 40 infants reported a statistically significant reduction in the length of hospital stay with surfactant therapy (mean difference -8 days, 95% CI -14 to -3 days). Heterogeneity testing was not applicable for this outcome. No statistically significant reductions were observed in other outcomes, including the duration of assisted ventilation, duration of supplemental oxygen, incidence of pneumothorax, pulmonary interstitial emphysema, air leaks, chronic lung disease, need for oxygen at discharge, or intraventricular hemorrhage. In conclusion, surfactant administration in infants with MAS may reduce the severity of respiratory illness and decrease the number of infants requiring ECMO for progressive respiratory failure. However, the relative effectiveness of surfactant therapy compared to, or in combination with, other treatment modalities such as inhaled nitric oxide, liquid ventilation, surfactant lavage, and high-frequency ventilation remains to be determined.
